These differ by the negative contribution −∑_{v:ord_v(x)>0} ord_v(x)log N(p_v), which is not O(1); e.g. x=2^n in Q gives difference −n log 2.

The proof invokes Dirichlet's unit theorem to assert that all Archimedean absolute values of an algebraic integer y are comparable: |y|_v≤c(κ)|y|_w. This is false. In Q(√2), the units y=(1+√2)^n have Archimedean absolute values (1+√2)^n and (√2−1)^n, whose ratio is unbounded. Hence the conclusion m(y,0)=O(1) is also false; for these units m(y,0) is asymptotic to h(y) and tends to infinity.

Theorem 1.5 (12) is stated with N(x,a_j), which counts valuations with multiplicity, but Eq. (21) replaces them by \overline{N}(x,a_j), which sums only distinct prime ideals (radical-type). This substitution is invalid. In the rational case the N-version gives log |a|+log |b|+log |c|, which yields only a trivial bound, not the radical bound claimed.

The theorem is false. Take a=1, b=2^{3^m}, c=2^{3^m}+1. Then a+b=c, the numbers are relatively prime, and a=1 has only prime factors of power 1. By LTE, v_3(c)=m+1, so rad(abc)=2 rad(c)≤2c/3^m. Therefore max(|a|,|b|,|c|)/rad(abc) ≥ 3^m/2, which is unbounded, contradicting the claimed uniform bound max≤C rad(abc).

Theorem 1.6 states a+b=c, but the proof says 'Since a+b+c=0' and uses the projective relation with a_2=-1. Under a+b=c, the relation for x=a/c is x−1=−b/c, so the corresponding point is 1, not −1. This is a sign inconsistency.
